source: Deng et al. (2024), Transportation Research Part F
key_supported_point: No single takeover time budget satisfies all scenarios; dynamic time budget is motivated.
project_role: Supports treating TOR budget as scenario-dependent rather than a fixed universal constant.

source: Liang, Calvert & van Lint (2026), IJHCI / Human Factors literature (via PubMed 42283150)
key_supported_point: Takeover time varies substantially across drivers/scenarios; sufficient time-budget design requires context.
project_role: Recent support for adaptive / contextual handover budgeting.

source: Roche, Thüring & Trukenbrod (2020), Accident Analysis & Prevention
key_supported_point: Drivers took over quickly but often braked/changed lane more strongly than necessary, increasing risk.
project_role: Supports fast takeover != safe recovery and motivates post-takeover recovery metrics.

source: One-pedal or two-pedal: Does the regenerative braking system improve driving safety? (2024)- ScienceDirect
key_supported_point: One-pedal mode did not change event perception but showed longer throttle-to-brake transition and more variable brake timing; safer than two-pedal in low urgency, less safe in high urgency.
project_role: Direct evidence that braking/control architecture can alter emergency control behaviour; motivates Experiment A profiles P2/P4.

source: Chen et al. (2021), Transportation Research Part F
key_supported_point: Driving experience affected takeover stability/adaptability, with interactions involving time budget and secondary task.
project_role: Supports later human-model / familiarity interaction work, but not a direct ICE-vs-EV prior claim.

source: Vigil, Kaayal & Szepelak (2023), SAE Technical Paper 2023-01-0623
sample_or_scope: Rivian R1T, Tesla Model Y/3, Hyundai Ioniq 5, VW ID.4, Ford Mustang Mach-E
key_supported_point: Production EVs show materially different regenerative deceleration behaviours; not all regen modes bring vehicles to a full stop.
project_role: Constrains generic EV-like braking profiles without requiring proprietary OEM maps. NOTE: exact numeric deceleration values not yet extracted from full text — paywalled; treat magnitudes as unverified until full-text retrieval.

source: A quantitative model of takeover request time budget for conditionally automated driving (2024), arXiv:2408.15682
sample_or_scope: not independently peer-reviewed at time of audit
key_supported_point: Proposes a formula estimating required TOR time budget from scenario variables.
project_role: Candidate formal structure for treating TOR budget as scenario-dependent rather than fixed; preprint status means findings are provisional.

source: A Systematic Review of Metrics Measuring Takeover Performance in Conditionally Automated Driving (2025)- International Journal of Human-Computer Interaction
key_supported_point: Catalogs and compares metrics used to quantify takeover performance across the field.
project_role: Informs candidate operational definitions for t_stabilise and N_correction so Phase 1 outcome metrics are not invented in isolation.

source: Post-Takeover Proficiency in Conditionally Automated Driving: Understanding Stabilization Time with Driving and Physiological Signals (2024)- Sensors 24(10):3193
key_supported_point: Driving-related stabilisation (steering, speed) is typically reached ~8-10 s after takeover; physiological recovery (heart rate, skin conductance) is slower and lags behind driving-metric stabilisation.
project_role: PRIMARY empirical anchor for freezing the Phase-0-checklist item ``define t_stabilise''; also cautions that a single-signal stabilisation definition may understate recovery time.

source: McDonald, Alambeigi, Engström, Markkula, Vogelpohl, Dunne & Yuma (2019), Human Factors
sample_or_scope: review of empirical and computational takeover literature
key_supported_point: Reviews cognitive and control-theoretic models of takeover braking/steering; notes existing manual-driving braking and steering models are treated as plausibly transferable to takeover modeling.
project_role: CLOSEST identified broad review to the project's mother question. Does not treat vehicle longitudinal-response architecture (regen/blended/delayed braking) as a systematically varied takeover factor -- used as the main comparator in the gap audit.

source: Characteristics of automatic emergency braking responses in passenger vehicles evaluated in the IIHS front crash prevention program (2023)- Accident Analysis & Prevention
key_supported_point: Different manufacturer AEB systems show measurably different braking-onset TTC thresholds, deceleration-rate scaling with speed (~0.6 m/s^2 per 10 km/h difference between superior- and basic-rated systems), and opposite jerk trends with speed.
project_role: STRONG real-world evidence that distinct control architectures (not vehicle mass or propulsion type) produce measurably different deceleration/jerk signatures. Supports the physical plausibility of Experiment A's P1-P4 profiles. This is AEB control behaviour, not human-driver takeover behaviour -- must not be over-extended to claim it is takeover evidence.

source: Sensorimotor adaptation when steering with altered vehicle dynamics (2018)- Transportation Research Part F
key_supported_point: Subtle steering-gain changes produce rapid adaptation with no after-effects; large/reversed gain changes produce slower adaptation and after-effects on return to baseline dynamics.
project_role: Direct empirical basis that mismatch effects are magnitude-dependent and non-linear -- informs how M_mismatch should eventually be parameterised (Gate C / D004) once the driver-vehicle mismatch branch is reopened.

source: The impact of electric vehicle's strong acceleration performance on traffic safety risks at signalized intersections: A case study in China (2025)- ScienceDirect
sample_or_scope: signalized intersections; EV vs ICE acceleration comparison
key_supported_point: EVs' stronger low-speed acceleration is associated with measurable shifts in TTC-based surrogate safety indicators at intersections.
project_role: Real-world evidence that acceleration-authority differences change kinematic risk exposure at the traffic-conflict level. Does NOT test human-fallback recovery margin after a hazard/TOR event -- it is traffic-conflict evidence, not takeover evidence. Motivates but does not establish the project's specific risk-state-escalation mechanism (Gate B).

source: A farewell to brake reaction times? Kinematics-dependent brake response in naturalistic rear-end emergencies (2017)- Accident Analysis & Prevention
key_supported_point: In naturalistic rear-end emergencies, brake onset is better predicted by kinematic looming/urgency thresholds than by a fixed reaction-time constant; onset is typically <1 s after threshold crossing, faster at higher urgency.
project_role: Directly challenges the Phase-1 simplifying assumption of a single fixed t_reaction. Should be logged as a named limitation of Phase 1A and a planned refinement for Phase 3 (reaction-time distributions).
